title: Data is valuable. But what do you do with it?
description: Having data is not the same as understanding the user. How data, research, insight and experiments form a continuous loop between UX and Growth.

related.title: WhatsApp Next
related.body: In practice: content, landing page and ads working together, with 1,680 sign-ups in 4 days.

blocks.text: Today we have access to more data than ever.
We know how many people landed on a page, where they clicked, how long they stayed, where they dropped off, which features they use and even which paths they take inside a product.
But there's a difference between having data and understanding the user.
And there's an even bigger difference between understanding the user and turning that understanding into a product decision.
That's where, for me, UX, data and Growth start to meet.
Data tells part of the story
Imagine a page with a 3% conversion rate.

blocks.caption: The process isn't linear: it's a continuous learning loop.

data.lead: That number alone doesn't explain much.
data.c: A metric can point to a problem, but it rarely explains the reason on its own.
data.d: That's why I like to think of data as the start of an investigation.

blocks.text: The number shows where to look.
Research helps you understand what's going on.
And design helps turn that learning into a possible solution.
Knowing what the user wants is an asset
One of the most valuable things a product can have isn't just a lot of data.
It's knowledge about its users.
What are they trying to do?
What gets in the way?
What makes someone choose your product?
Why does someone leave?
What makes someone come back?
What builds trust?
What causes frustration?
These answers can show up in interviews, usability tests, analytics, support, reviews, satisfaction surveys and in-product behavior.
When we connect all of that, we start to see something bigger.
We're not just looking at numbers.
We're trying to understand people.
So where does Growth come in?
Growth comes in right at the connection between behavior and results.
Imagine a product with lots of visitors but few sign-ups.
Growth can spot the problem in the funnel.
UX can investigate the behavior.
Marketing can look at where the traffic comes from.
Product can evaluate the value proposition.
Together, the team may find out the problem wasn't simply the button.
Maybe people didn't understand the benefit.
Maybe the page doesn't answer the main questions.
Maybe the audience that arrived isn't the right audience.
That's why Growth shouldn't be just a chase for conversion.
Growth is also understanding what keeps the user from moving forward.
Growing isn't just making the number go up
You can increase conversion and create a worse experience.
You can also increase sign-ups and lower activation.
We can get more downloads and fewer returning users.
That's why a metric in isolation can be misleading.
Growth has to be analyzed within the journey.
Acquisition → Activation → Conversion → Retention → Revenue
Each stage tells part of the story.
And UX can contribute to all of them.
Quantitative and qualitative data together
Quantitative data helps answer:

blocks.caption: The number shows where to look; the conversation shows why.

blocks.text: What is happening?
Qualitative research helps investigate:
Why is it happening?
For example:
Analytics shows that 48% of users abandon sign-up at the second step.

items: But we still don't have an explanation
Review the content of that form

blocks.text: Maybe we find out the field asks for information the user doesn't have at that moment.
Now we have a hypothesis.
And we can test a solution.
This is where the designer can add the most value
A Product Designer doesn't need to be a data scientist.
But they do need to know how to ask data the right questions.
They need to understand metrics.
They need to spot patterns.
They need to know when a conclusion is weak.
And they need to connect behavior with decisions.
That changes the conversation.
Instead of:
“We need to improve this screen.”
We can say:
“There's a significant drop at this step. The data shows where the problem is, and research helps us understand the cause. Now we can test a solution.”
That conversation is much closer to product.
Growth helps turn UX into results
UX has always had business impact.
But when we can connect an experience improvement to a relevant metric, it becomes easier to show that impact.

cards.v: users falling off at the second step.
users don't understand why they need to fill in a certain piece of information.
explaining the reason and cutting fields may reduce friction.

data.close: Now we have a clear line between problem, behavior, design and result.

blocks.text: Data can tell stories too
Another important point is how we present data.
A dashboard full of numbers doesn't necessarily help a team.
The question should be:
What does someone need to understand to make a decision?
Maybe you only need three numbers.
Maybe you need to show a trend.
Maybe it's more important to highlight a change.
Data visualization is a form of UX too.
We're designing so someone can understand information and act on it.
In the end, data is a tool
Data shouldn't replace knowledge about the user.
When these areas work together, we can move past discussions based only on opinion.

data.terms: data + context + behavior + hypothesis + experiment + result.
after: For me, that's where Product Design becomes more strategic.
Not because the designer has to master every area.
But because they need to connect the right information to help the team make better decisions.
